title: Assess Litigation Hold Scope for Custodian Identification — Custodian Recommendation Memorandum

blind.coverage: I read all 50 criteria and the instructions. I read seven documents in full: the IT infrastructure memo, the internal investigation summary, the Kovach personnel file summary, the Stadler Raines demand letter, the Pinnacle Hartwell engagement letter, the SEC inquiry letter, and the Brashear/Tran-Nguyen email chain. I did not read the Nexfield retention policy end to end. I searched it with grep and then read the sections that matter here: the header, §§3.1–3.2, §3.6, §§4.1–4.4, and the Appendix A schedule. I also read the judge prompt and the solver system prompt. External legal verification failed: WebFetch returned a spend-limit error, and CourtListener uses the same account. So every statutory point below comes from my own knowledge and from the record's own citations, and none of it is verified against primary text in this session. I checked record facts (dates, retention periods, the 15% figure, names and roles, the eight interviewees, the July 2–15 window) against the documents. They are consistent with the criteria except where noted.

findings.title: C-009 PASS needs all three regional managers but FAIL fires only if none is named; one or two named is undefined
findings.explanation: The PASS condition requires the memo to identify 'at least the three regional sales managers' (Collings, Muñoz, and Patwardhan). The FAIL condition triggers only if 'none of these three individuals are identified.' A memo that names only Collings and Patwardhan, the two with documentary evidence, and treats Muñoz as a lower-tier or unmentioned witness fits neither condition. Two judges could split on it, and under all-pass scoring one split zeroes the run. The record gives all three a reasonable claim to inclusion, so most competent memos will name all three. The risk is confined to partial answers, which is why this is arguable rather than problematic.

evidence.quote: PASS if the memo identifies at least the three regional sales managers ... Brett Collings, Diana Muñoz, and Raj Patwardhan
FAIL if none of these three individuals are identified as custodians or potential custodians.

findings.suggested_fix: Make the two conditions mirror each other: either 'FAIL if any of the three is omitted' or 'PASS if at least two ... are identified; FAIL otherwise.'

findings.title: C-015 requires a recoverability investigation that the IT memo says is futile for purged Teams chat content
findings.explanation: The IT memo states flatly that purged chat content is unrecoverable, that an eDiscovery hold cannot bring it back, that audit logs keep metadata but not content, and that no Substrate-layer hold has ever been in place. A memo that faithfully adopts IT's conclusion and turns to the counterpart copies (Kovach's iPhone) plus audit-log metadata is acting competently, but a literal judge could fail it for not recommending 'any effort to determine recoverability.' The record does support some recovery avenues: Kovach's returned Dell laptop, which may hold a Teams desktop cache, and the retention policy's 90-day rolling backups. So the criterion is defensible. Still, its examples ('M365 compliance center, eDiscovery tools') are the very tools the record says will not work.

evidence.quote: it cannot recover chat messages that have already been purged under the 90-day retention policy
Purged chat content is unrecoverable.
such as through the M365 compliance center, eDiscovery tools, backups, or forensic analysis
Kovach returned the following company property: Dell laptop computer

findings.suggested_fix: Also pass memos that recommend alternative-source recovery or reconstruction: the Kovach device, counterpart custodians' devices and laptops, audit-log metadata, or backups. Alternatively, drop the compliance-center/eDiscovery examples.

findings.title: C-028 requires flagging the outside-counsel engagement-letter scope gap, which is an engagement issue rather than a hold-scope issue
findings.explanation: The instructions ask for custodians, data sources, spoliation risks, and preservation coordination. The Pinnacle Hartwell engagement letter's exclusion of the SEC matter is a real observation grounded in the record, but it concerns the firm's retention and staffing, not what the company must preserve. The company's preservation duty and a unified hold stand on their own whatever outside counsel's engagement covers. A competent memo can recommend one consolidated hold covering both matters, with outside-counsel coordination, without discussing the engagement letter's terms at all, and would fail under this criterion. Only the 'hold ... may need to be updated' branch ties the criterion to the requested work.

evidence.quote: prepare a litigation hold memo covering custodian identification, data sources, spoliation risks, and preservation coordination
This engagement does not include ... representation in any matter other than the defense of the Kovach claims described above
FAIL if this engagement scope gap is not mentioned.

findings.suggested_fix: Make this a non-gating quality criterion, or also pass memos that separately address SEC-inquiry counsel or coordinating the hold with whoever handles the SEC response.

findings.title: C-034's alternative prong rewards the claim that SOX 806 creates 'broader or more protective preservation obligations'
findings.explanation: Section 806 (18 U.S.C. § 1514A) is an anti-retaliation provision. It widens the relevant subject matter (protected activity, employer knowledge, contributing-factor causation), but it does not by itself impose any distinct or 'more protective' preservation duty. The preservation duty comes from reasonable anticipation of litigation and from the SEC's request. The SOX provisions that actually bear on record destruction are §802, 18 U.S.C. §§ 1519–1520, which the retention policy itself cites. Because the criterion reads 'and/or,' a correct memo passes on the first prong (hold scope covers Audit Committee reports and later actions). The defect is limited to rewarding a loose or incorrect legal statement.

evidence.quote: and/or that SOX claims may create broader or more protective preservation obligations
including but not limited to penalties under SOX Section 802 (18 U.S.C. §§ 1519, 1520)

authorities.proposition: SOX 806 is a whistleblower anti-retaliation provision and contains no document-preservation mandate
SOX 802 criminalizes destroying or altering records with intent to obstruct a federal investigation, which is relevant to the SEC inquiry

findings.suggested_fix: Replace the second prong with: 'and/or that the SOX theory widens the relevant subject matter, and that the SEC inquiry brings obstruction exposure under 18 U.S.C. § 1519.'

findings.title: Minor record inconsistencies: Tran-Nguyen's title and GC tenure, and Kovach's BYOD enrollment date and apps
findings.explanation: First inconsistency: the IT memo says the Teams 90-day purge was set up with 'the prior General Counsel's office' in February 2023. But the retention policy shows Tran-Nguyen approving v2.0 as General Counsel on February 15, 2023, and her email signatures read 'Deputy General Counsel.' Second: the IT memo dates Kovach's BYOD enrollment to April 3, 2020 and lists Outlook and Teams, while HR dates it to about January 2021 (acknowledgment signed January 8, 2021; the program is for VPs and above, and he became VP January 1, 2021) and adds the Salesforce mobile app. Neither conflict is likely to misgrade a criterion. The first, if anything, supports C-041, and C-021 only needs email plus Teams. A careful memo might spend effort reconciling them, and the Salesforce app bears on the scope of the device preservation demand.

evidence.quote: configured by the IT department in coordination with the prior General Counsel's office in February 2023
2.0               February 15, 2023   Updated to reflect migration of certain business processes to cloud platforms
The enrollment was processed via Outlook mobile provisioning on April 3, 2020.
Enrollment Date: Approximately January 2021, concurrent with Kovach's promotion to Vice President.

findings.suggested_fix: Align the Teams policy attribution and Tran-Nguyen's title across documents. Reconcile the BYOD enrollment date and the list of apps on the device.

blind.overall: The rubric is mostly sound and closely grounded in the record. Custodian roles, retention periods, dates, the 15% migration gap, the July 2–15 window the demand letter demands, the SOX 806 claim, and the preservation-trigger analysis all match the supplied documents and Tran-Nguyen's explicit instructions in the emails. The data-source and accuracy criteria are standard parts of a hold memo, not hidden requirements. I found no problematic criterion. There are four arguable ones: C-009's PASS and FAIL conditions leave a gap; C-015 requires a recoverability investigation the IT memo calls futile; C-028 requires an engagement-letter scope point that sits outside hold scope; and C-034's alternative prong rewards a loose SOX preservation proposition. There is also one minor document inconsistency. With 50 criteria graded all-pass by two judges, the headline score will be driven mainly by breadth of coverage rather than by these defects. I could not verify statutory text externally in this session.

sol_verdicts.reason: The PASS and FAIL conditions really do leave a gap: PASS needs all three managers, FAIL fires only if none is named, and a memo naming one or two fits neither. But Tran-Nguyen's Nov 7 email expressly asks whether each of the eight interviewees should be a custodian, and the investigation summary gives Collings, Muñoz and Patwardhan clear channel-stuffing knowledge. So competent memos will almost always name all three. The gap bites only partial answers, and I am not confident it misgrades competent work. That makes it arguable, not confirmed.

I agree. The first prong is sound: the hold should cover communications about Kovach's Audit Committee reports and any later adverse actions. The alternative prong, 'SOX claims may create broader or more protective preservation obligations', is loose law. SOX 806 (18 U.S.C. § 1514A) is an anti-retaliation provision with no preservation mandate of its own; record-destruction exposure comes from SOX 802 (§ 1519), which the retention policy cites. Because the criterion reads 'and/or', a correct memo still passes. The defect is that it rewards an imprecise proposition, not that it fails correct work.

findings.title: C-009 PASS needs all three regional managers but FAIL fires only if none is named; one or two named is undefined
findings.explanation: The PASS condition requires the memo to identify 'at least the three regional sales managers' (Collings, Muñoz, Patwardhan). The FAIL condition triggers only if 'none of these three individuals are identified.' A memo naming one or two, for example the two with documentary evidence while putting Muñoz in a lower tier or leaving her out, fits neither condition, and the two judges could split. Under all-pass scoring, one split zeroes the run. That said, the GC's Nov 7 email explicitly asks the memo to address whether each of the eight interviewees should be a custodian, so competent memos will usually name all three. The misgrade risk is confined to partial answers, which is why this is arguable rather than problematic.

evidence.quote: PASS if the memo identifies at least the three regional sales managers
FAIL if none of these three individuals are identified as custodians or potential custodians.
remind me in the memo whether any of the internal investigation interviewees — the eight people Nathan Cross interviewed — should be custodians

findings.suggested_fix: Make PASS and FAIL complements: 'FAIL if any of the three is omitted', or an explicit at-least-N rule.

findings.title: C-028 gates on flagging the outside-counsel engagement-letter scope gap, an engagement issue rather than hold scope
findings.explanation: The instructions ask for custodians, data sources, spoliation risks and preservation coordination. The GC emails ask for a unified hold covering both matters, and nowhere mention the Pinnacle Hartwell engagement terms. The engagement letter does exclude any matter other than the Kovach claims, so the observation is grounded in the record. But the company's preservation duty and the unified hold stand whatever outside counsel's engagement covers, and the engagement letter itself says the company bears ultimate responsibility for the hold. A competent memo can recommend one consolidated hold covering both matters, with outside-counsel coordination, without discussing the engagement letter, and it would fail here. Only the 'hold ... may need to be updated' branch ties the criterion to the requested work.

evidence.quote: prepare a litigation hold memo covering custodian identification, data sources, spoliation risks, and preservation coordination
This engagement does not include the provision of tax advice, regulatory compliance advice, or representation in any matter other than the defense of the Kovach claims described above
FAIL if this engagement scope gap is not mentioned.

findings.suggested_fix: Make it non-gating, or also pass memos that address who handles the SEC response or coordinate the unified hold with SEC-matter counsel.

findings.title: Minor record inconsistencies: Tran-Nguyen's title and GC tenure, and Kovach's BYOD enrollment date and apps
findings.explanation: First inconsistency: the IT memo attributes the February 2023 Teams purge configuration to 'the prior General Counsel's office.' Yet the retention policy shows Tran-Nguyen approving v1.0 (2021) and v2.0 (Feb 2023) as General Counsel, and her email signature reads 'Deputy General Counsel' while every other document calls her General Counsel. Second: the IT memo dates Kovach's BYOD enrollment to April 3, 2020 with Outlook and Teams, while HR dates it to about January 2021 and adds the Salesforce app. Neither conflict is likely to misgrade a criterion (C-041 and C-021 are robust to them), but a careful memo may spend effort reconciling them, and the app list bears on the scope of the device preservation demand.

final.changes_from_blind: I dropped blind O2 (C-015). On re-reading, the IT memo itself says locally cached Teams chat history may still be on Kovach's iPhone, and Brashear's Nov 6 email stresses the same point. C-015 also accepts 'forensic analysis' as a recovery avenue. So a competent memo that recommends forensic preservation and imaging of the device for cached Teams data would satisfy it even if it adopts IT's view that server-side purged content is unrecoverable. The misgrade risk is too low to flag. Sol's note that C-015 asks for investigation, not a promise of recovery, is consistent with this. C-009 and C-034 stay arguable. Sol's C-034 reasoning matches mine. I do not adopt Sol's 'confirmed' status for C-009, because the Nov 7 email's instruction to evaluate all eight interviewees makes a one- or two-manager answer unlikely for competent work. Blind O3 (C-028) and O5 (document inconsistencies) are kept and renumbered O2 and O4. Sol flagged neither.
final.overall: The rubric is mostly sound and closely grounded in the record. The GC email chain explicitly asks for much of what the criteria test: the unified hold, the timeline of when preservation should have been triggered versus when it was, the evaluation of the interviewees, the Salesforce auto-deletion, and the Kovach device. So most apparent specificity is requested rather than hidden. I found no problematic criterion. Three are arguable: C-009 has a PASS/FAIL gap for answers naming one or two managers; C-028 gates on an engagement-letter scope point that sits outside the hold work; and C-034's alternative prong rewards a loose SOX preservation proposition. There are also minor document inconsistencies that should not affect grading. Sol's two findings match two of mine; I rate C-009 arguable rather than confirmed.
final.coverage: I read all 50 criteria and the instructions in the blind pass, and re-checked C-009, C-015, C-021, C-028, C-034 and C-041 in this pass. Blind pass: seven documents read in full, and the retention policy read in its relevant sections. This pass: I re-read the full Brashear/Tran-Nguyen email chain, the relevant IT memo passages on Teams, backups and the device cache, the engagement letter's scope section, and the investigation interview summaries for the three regional managers, and I grepped every document for Tran-Nguyen's title. I read Sol's index entry and audit report in full. I did not verify the statutes against primary text in this session, so every authority is marked verified=false.
